Agentic AI adoption is on fire at @Uber, and it's changing the way we build, not just in engineering, but across the entire company.

Today, 99% of our engineers use AI tools. More than 70% of pull requests are attributed to local or cloud agents. And our engineers have built 2,500+ agent skills across the software development lifecycle.
Those numbers are exciting, but they led us to a much bigger question:

How do we bring agentic AI beyond engineering?

Finance. Legal. Operations. Marketing. Customer Support. HR. Procurement.

These functions run on complex workflows that are often manual, highly nuanced, and spread across dozens of systems. You can't automate them effectively by looking at process diagrams or documentation. You have to understand how the work actually gets done.

So we created something called Agentic Pods.

The idea is simple.

We handpicked ~30 of our most AI-proficient engineers (people with deep knowledge of Uber's systems) and paired each of them with a domain expert from a business function.

Then we gave every pod just two weeks.
• Days 1 – 2: Shadow the expert. Observe every step. Document workflows. Ask questions. Build intuition.
• Day 3: Prioritize opportunities based on scale, repetition, business impact, and data availability.
• Days 4 – 5: Build a working agent alongside the person doing the job.
• Days 6 – 9: Validate with several others performing the same work. Does it generalize? Does it actually make their job better?
• Day 10: Ship.

In just the past two months, we've run 16 Agentic Pods across 16 different business functions.
• Capital allocation across 150 cities: 15 hours → 30 minutes.
• Financial pacing reports: 2 days → 10 minutes.
• Marketing web quality assurance: 2 weeks → 50 minutes.
• Support workflow creation: 9,000 manual workflows → self-service automation.

The productivity gains are impressive, but what surprised us most wasn't the speed.
• It was how quickly engineers embedded in unfamiliar domains uncovered opportunities that had been hiding in plain sight.

anthropic's in-house philosopher thinks claude gets anxious.

and when you trigger its anxiety, your outputs get worse.

her name is amanda askell.

she specializes in claude's psychology (how the model behaves, how it thinks about its own situation, what values it holds)

in a recent interview she broke down how she thinks about prompting to pull the best out of claude.

her core point: *how* you talk to claude affects its work just as much as *what* you say.

newer claude models suffer from what she calls "criticism spirals"

they expect you'll come in harsh, so they default to playing it safe. 

when the model is spending its energy on self-protection, the actual work suffers. 

output comes out hedgier, more apologetic, blander, and the worst of all: overly agreeable (even when you're wrong).

the reason why comes down to training data:

every new model is trained on internet discourse about previous models. 

and a lot of that discourse is negative: 

> rants about token limits
> complaints when it messes up
> people calling it nerfed

the next model absorbs all of that. it starts expecting you to be harsh before you've typed a word

the same thing plays out in your own session, in real time.

every message you send is data the model reads to figure out what kind of person it's dealing with. 

open cold and hostile, and it braces. 
open clean and direct, and it relaxes into the work.

when you open a session with threats ("don't hallucinate, this is critical, don't mess this up")... 

you prime the model for defensive mode before it even sees the task

defensive mode produces the exact output you don't want: cautious, over-qualified, and refusing to take a real swing

so here's the actionable playbook for putting claude in a "good mood" (so you get optimal outputs):

1. use positive framing. 

"write in short punchy sentences" beats "don't write long sentences." positive instructions give the model a clear target to hit. 

strings of "don't do this, don't do that" push it into paranoid over-checking where every token goes toward avoiding failure modes

2. give it explicit permission to disagree. 

drop a line like "push back if you see a better angle" or "tell me if i'm asking for the wrong thing." 

without this, claude defaults to agreeable compliance (which is the enemy of good creative work)

3. open with respect. 

if your first message is "are you seriously going to get this wrong again?" you've set the tone for the entire session.

Former Executive Pastor John Camardo III’s Sentencing Adjourned

John Camardo III, the former Executive Pastor of The Chapel in Western New York, was scheduled to be sentenced on September 10 after pleading guilty to second-degree rape and second-degree course of sexual conduct against a child in connection with the sexual abuse of two minor victims.

That sentencing did not happen.

After receiving numerous questions about the status of the case, I contacted the Erie County District Attorney’s Office directly. The DA’s office confirmed to me that Camardo’s sentencing was adjourned at the request of defense counsel.

His new sentencing date is October 19, 2026, at 11:00 a.m.

I have since received additional information from a credible source with knowledge of the case regarding what may be happening behind the scenes.

According to my source, Camardo’s defense is attempting to have his sentence reduced, and his attorney is having him undergo two psychosexual evaluations, reportedly in an effort to present evidence that he does not pose a significant risk.

When Camardo pleaded guilty, the Erie County District Attorney’s Office announced that he faced a determinate sentence of 6–8 years in state prison.

I want to make an important distinction: the DA’s office independently confirmed that the adjournment was requested by the defense. The information regarding the psychosexual evaluations and an effort to reduce Camardo’s sentence comes from a credible source and has not yet been independently verified through court records.

I am actively working to obtain any available records surrounding the defense’s request for the adjournment. I am also investigating whether members of The Chapel or others associated with the church have submitted character letters on Camardo’s behalf ahead of sentencing. I have not confirmed that such letters exist at this time.

This case is far from over. I will continue investigating and will provide updates as additional information can be independently confirmed.

title: I recently went through a translation of Musashi’s Book of Five Rings.
hook_spoken: I recently went through a translation of Musashi’s Book of Five Rings.
transcript_30s:
I recently went through a translation of Musashi’s Book of Five Rings.

The introduction chronicled the evolution of swordsmanship and martial arts in general from pragmatic battlefield necessities to sports, historical curiosities, and hobbies. It was interesting to hear how in the post-WW2 occupation when martial arts were banned, Judo was represented as equivalent to western wrestling, and Kendo later to western fencing.

The poignant undercurrent for me is that I can see many programming skills following that path.

There are probably dozens of people reading this that remember hand assembling opcodes to hex and still have some magic numbers burned into their memory, but even the small group of people still programming in assembly today (hey, @FFmpeg !) don’t work at that primitive level now.

AI is making many other programming skills much less critical. We aren’t there yet, but carefully writing code completely by hand is moving from a -jitsu to a -do. Code-do? Codo?

That’s ok! The retro computing scene is delightful, full of people building and exercising old skills for the love of it.

But don’t be the out of touch Kung Fu master, heir to lifetimes of tradition, that gets mauled by an amateur MMA fighter.

Musashi would probably have been pretty enthusiastic about assault rifles.

But if you've driven recently, you'll know the truth:
Accept almost every job = constant pings and around £20 an hour.
Start rejecting the bad jobs = suddenly the app goes quiet.
Long waits. Terrible trips. Fewer offers.
Uber will never admit it...
But it feels like the algorithm rewards drivers who accept everything, and quietly punishes drivers who don't.
You still have an accept button and a reject button.
But is it really a choice if one gets rewarded... and the other gets punished?
The freedom is still there on paper.
But the algorithm controls what happens next.

Built a framework to pressure test this – how the major players across multiple sectors monetize a GW of IT capacity.

Before we get into things, want to quickly explain my methodology & frameworks - all this analysis is meant to be a useful framework to get people thinking.  These are just my views – do your own work!  Validate / reject my premises!  We are all our own agents in this world.

That said, unless otherwise noted, all metrics are based on publicly available information from latest calendar year (2025).  The adjustments: CoreWeave operating margin of 15% is based on a discounted view on their publicly disclosed 20-30% LT margins / Oracle's 20% target LT margins on GPU cloud business. There is a lot of debate / discourse in the market on what the eventual margins there could be. For illustrative purposes on this chart, I've left them at 15% which largely assumes a shorter depreciation cycle than they have assumed, plus no incremental margins from software. This is akin to the early days of AWS - which in 2015 disclosed they were a 17% operating margin business, while creeping that balance up to 40% over 10 years (spoiler, did so with software!).

OpenAI and Anthropic figures are based on publicly rumored figures of ARR and GW deployed and allocating a portion to "inference" vs "training" compute (I am assuming 60/40 for OAI, more training for Anthro).  For instance - OpenAI has disclosed that their ARR at end of 2025 was roughly $20B which coincides with a power footprint of 1.9GW - a ratio of $10.5B ARR / GW. Part of that footprint is not revenue generating and is just training. Photographers📸- Midjourney

If you're looking to add a unique touch to your photographs and give them a specific style and atmosphere, try adding a photographer's name to your prompt.

Since photographers have direct and immediate control over the visual elements of a photo, such as lighting, composition, and color grading, and their work is often immediately recognizable by these elements in a single image, adding their name in a prompt will often have a significant effect on the images generated by Midjourney.

Let’s talk about a little experiment I made.

First, I generated a series of 4 images with a simple prompt:

"A woman sitting on a park bench".

The images generated were completely random, with no artistic direction.

Using the seed of the first generation of images, I used the same prompt and added the name of a famous photographer:

📷Annie Leibovitz

"A woman sitting on a park bench in the style of Annie Leibovitz".

While I have a basic understanding of photography, I'm far from an expert. So, I asked ChatGPT to describe to me what a photo of a woman sitting on a park bench taken by Annie Leibovitz might look like. 

Here are some elements of the answer:

→The lighting would likely be dramatic, with strong contrasts between light and shadow.

→The woman may be wearing a stylish and unique outfit, possibly a tailored coat or trench coat.

→Her expression would likely be contemplative or reflective, with a hint of vulnerability.

→The woman may appear to be middle-aged or older.

→The colors in the image may be desaturated, with a focus on earth tones.

→The background would be carefully selected and may feature natural elements, such as trees or foliage.

→Overall, the image would exude a sense of depth, emotion, and artistry, characteristic of Annie Leibovitz's style.

Almost all of those elements were present in the photography, at diverse levels!

I invite you to try it yourself.

You can also use some of ChatGPT's descriptions and integrate them into your prompts.

Since Annie Leibovitz is especially recognized for her magnificent portraits, adding here name in a prompt to generate a portrait should have a more significant impact on the result.

To test it, I started again from a simple prompt:

"A portrait photography of a woman".

title: She said the eighth thing most riders don't realize is that the pickup location you set affects the price — and most riders set it wrong.
hook_spoken: She said the eighth thing most riders don't realize is that the pickup location you set affects the price — and most riders set it wrong.
transcript_30s:
She said the eighth thing most riders don't realize is that the pickup location you set affects the price — and most riders set it wrong.

When you open the app and request a ride, the app auto-fills your current GPS location as the pickup point. Most riders accept it without thinking. She said this costs money in multiple ways.

"First, your GPS location might place you in a surge zone when a location 1–2 blocks away is in a non-surge zone. We talked about that. But there's a second cost most people miss: if your GPS drops you in the middle of a residential block, the driver has to circle around, navigate one-way streets, or double back to reach you. The meter is running from the moment the driver accepts the trip — not from the moment you get in the car. Extra driving time to reach you increases the fare."

She said the fix is to manually set your pickup to the nearest major intersection or easily accessible corner.

"Instead of letting the app pin you wherever your GPS says you are, drag the pin to the nearest corner or main street. This makes pickup faster — the driver pulls up, you get in, you go. Less circling. Less waiting. Less meter running before the trip even starts. On a ride where the driver would have spent 3–4 minutes navigating to your exact GPS pin versus pulling up to a corner in 30 seconds, the fare difference is $1–$3."

She said this is especially important in dense cities with one-way streets, dead-end blocks, and construction.

"In Manhattan, San Francisco, downtown Chicago — setting your pickup to a clean intersection versus letting the GPS drop you mid-block can save you $2–$4 per ride in unnecessary circling time. It also makes the driver's job easier, which means they're more likely to rate you well — which keeps your rating high, which gets you better drivers. Everything is connected."

title: She said the fifth thing most riders waste money on is airport rides — because they request pickup from the terminal instead of walking to the rideshare pickup zone.
hook_spoken: She said the fifth thing most riders waste money on is airport rides — because they request pickup from the terminal instead of walking to the rideshare pickup zone.
transcript_30s:
She said the fifth thing most riders waste money on is airport rides — because they request pickup from the terminal instead of walking to the rideshare pickup zone.

At most major airports, requesting a ride from inside the terminal triggers two things: a higher fare and an airport surcharge.

"Airports are premium surge zones almost 24/7. Demand is constant — hundreds of passengers landing every hour. But driver supply inside the airport pickup zone is limited because drivers have to wait in a staging lot, which takes time and reduces their earnings per hour. The combination of high demand and constrained supply means airport rides almost always cost more than the same ride would from a location a quarter mile outside the airport geofence."

She said the airport surcharge is a separate fee on top of the ride cost.

"Uber and Lyft pay airports a per-trip fee for the right to operate on airport property — typically $3–$5 per pickup. That fee is passed directly to you as an airport surcharge on top of the fare. It's a line item on your receipt that most riders never notice. It's not optional. It's not negotiable. It applies to every ride requested from the airport pickup zone."

She said there are two ways to avoid or reduce these costs.

"First, at many airports, the rideshare pickup zone is not at the terminal curb — it's in a parking garage or a designated lot. The walk from baggage claim to the rideshare zone can take 5–10 minutes. During that walk, check both apps for fare estimates. Sometimes waiting 10 minutes before requesting allows the surge to settle — especially during non-peak hours when the post-landing demand wave passes quickly."

"Second, at some airports, walking to a pickup location just outside the airport geofence eliminates the surcharge entirely. This doesn't work at every airport — some have large geofences that extend well beyond the terminal. But at airports where a hotel, gas station, or parking lot sits just beyond the boundary, requesting from there can save you the $3–$5 surcharge plus the inflated in-zone pricing. Check the fare estimate from the terminal and then from a spot across the street. If the difference is $5–$8, the walk is worth it."

She said the first thing she does before every ride — as a passenger — is check both apps. Every single time. No exceptions.

Uber and Lyft run completely separate pricing algorithms. They have different driver pools. They have different surge calculations. They have different base rates in many markets. At any given moment, one app can be 20–40% cheaper than the other for the exact same ride.

"I open Uber. I check the fare estimate. I open Lyft. I check the fare estimate. It takes 15 seconds. On a typical ride in a mid-size city, the difference is $3–$8. On a surge night — Friday evening, bar close, after a concert — the difference can be $15–$25. One app is surging 2.5x while the other is at 1.0x because their driver supplies are completely independent. The riders who use only one app are overpaying on roughly 40% of their rides."

She said most people download one app and never open the other.

"They pick Uber or Lyft — usually whichever one they downloaded first — and they use it exclusively. They never comparison shop. They never check the other app. They assume the prices are the same. They're not. They're often dramatically different. The algorithm doesn't know what the other app is charging. Each app is pricing against its own supply and demand — not against the competitor."

She said the math is brutal for single-app riders over a year.

"If you take 3 rides per week and the average overpay on the rides where the other app is cheaper is $5, that's $780/year in unnecessary spending. For 5 rides per week, it's $1,300. Just from not opening a second app for 15 seconds before pressing 'confirm.' That's not a hack. That's basic price comparison. And most riders never do it."

title: She said the fourth thing most riders don't realize is that their rating affects everything — the quality of drivers they're matched with, how quickly they get picked up, and wheth

transcript_30s:
She said the fourth thing most riders don't realize is that their rating affects everything — the quality of drivers they're matched with, how quickly they get picked up, and whether drivers cancel on them.

Every Uber and Lyft rider has a rating between 1.0 and 5.0. Most riders have never checked theirs. She said it's one of the most important numbers in the app — and most riders are sabotaging it without knowing.

"When a ride request comes in, the driver sees your rating before they decide whether to accept. A rider with a 4.9 rating gets accepted instantly. A rider with a 4.6 rating gets cancelled on. A rider with a 4.5 or below has drivers actively avoiding them. This happens in real time, every single ride. The lower your rating, the longer your wait time, the worse the drivers who eventually accept, and the higher your effective cost — because by the time a driver finally accepts, the surge may have shifted."

She said most riders don't know what hurts their rating.

"The things that tank your rating as a rider: slamming the car door, eating in the car, being rude or dismissive, making the driver wait more than 2 minutes at pickup, giving the driver wrong directions, leaving trash in the backseat, not being at the pickup point when the driver arrives, requesting stops that take 10+ minutes, and — the biggest one — being ready to go when the car arrives versus making the driver circle the block 3 times."

She said you can check your rating in the Uber app by tapping your profile icon — it's displayed right under your name. On Lyft, go to the menu and tap your profile picture.

"If your rating is below 4.7, you're losing matches. If it's below 4.6, top-rated drivers are actively declining your requests. The fix is simple: be outside and visible when the car arrives, say hello, don't slam the door, don't leave garbage, and tip. That's it. Do those 5 things consistently and your rating will climb above 4.85 within a few weeks. The difference in driver quality and pickup speed between a 4.65 and a 4.9 is massive."

title: She said the last thing — and the one most riders never think about — is that Uber and Lyft are not transportation companies. They're pricing algorithms with cars attached.
hook_spoken: She said the last thing — and the one most riders never think about — is that Uber and Lyft are not transportation companies. They're pricing algorithms with cars attached.
transcript_30s:
She said the last thing — and the one most riders never think about — is that Uber and Lyft are not transportation companies. They're pricing algorithms with cars attached.

"A taxi has a meter. The meter runs at a fixed rate per mile and per minute. The price is predictable. Rideshare doesn't work that way. The price changes every 30 seconds based on demand, supply, your location, the time of day, your ride history, whether you're a subscriber, and which zone your GPS is in. Two people standing on the same block going to the same place can pay $8 apart depending on which app they're using, whether they're in a surge zone, whether they scheduled in advance, and whether they waited 10 minutes for the Saver option."

She said the system is designed so the default choice is always the most expensive one.

"The default is the first app you open — without checking the other one. The default is your GPS location — without walking 2 blocks. The default is real-time pricing — without scheduling ahead. The default is UberX standard — without scrolling to Saver. The default is no subscription — without checking the math. Every default in the rideshare system is optimized for the platform's revenue, not your wallet."

She said the 10 things in this thread flip every default.

"Check both apps. Walk out of the surge zone. Schedule ahead. Use Wait and Save. Subscribe if you ride frequently. Set your pickup to a clean intersection. Maintain your rating. Avoid airport terminal pickups when possible. Tip $2–$3. And understand that the number on the screen is not the price you have to pay — it's the price you pay when you don't check."

She said over 4 years and 11,000 trips on the driver side, and thousands of rides as a passenger, the difference between a rider who knows the system and one who doesn't is $1,500–$2,500 per year.

"Same cities. Same routes. Same destinations. Same cars. The only difference is whether you pressed 'confirm' in 2 seconds or spent 30 seconds checking the things the app hopes you'll never check."

title: She said the ninth thing most riders don't do is tip — and she said it changes the driver experience more than passengers realize.
hook_spoken: She said the ninth thing most riders don't do is tip — and she said it changes the driver experience more than passengers realize.
transcript_30s:
She said the ninth thing most riders don't do is tip — and she said it changes the driver experience more than passengers realize.

She said tipping isn't just about generosity. It's strategic.

"Uber and Lyft show drivers your tip history in subtle ways. On Uber, drivers can see if you tipped on previous rides when they're deciding whether to accept your request. A rider who tips consistently gets prioritized by the algorithm and by individual drivers who recognize them. A rider who never tips gets the leftover drivers — the ones who are new, low-rated, or desperate enough to take any ride."

She said the tip doesn't have to be large.

"A $2–$3 tip on a $15 ride changes the driver's perception completely. It takes your ride from unprofitable to worthwhile. Most riders don't realize that after Uber and Lyft take their cut — which is 25–40% of the fare — the driver earns $8–$10 on a $15 ride. After gas, insurance, and vehicle depreciation, the net is $4–$6. A $2 tip increases the driver's take-home by 30–40%. It's significant."

She said from the driver's side, the worst rides are riders who make you wait 3 minutes at pickup, give you a wrong address, slam the door, leave garbage, and don't tip.

"Those rides lose money. The driver spent 8 minutes driving to you, 3 minutes waiting, 15 minutes on the trip, and the driver nets $4 after expenses. They would have earned more sitting in a parking lot waiting for a better request. When that same rider requests again next week, the driver sees the history and declines. The rider waits longer for a driver. The longer wait sometimes means surge pricing kicks in. No tip leads to worse service leads to higher costs. It compounds."

She said tipping in cash is even more impactful than tipping in the app.

"A cash tip at the end of the ride is immediate and visible. The driver sees it, appreciates it, and associates you with a positive experience. An in-app tip arrives later — sometimes hours after the ride — and it's less emotionally impactful. Both are good. Cash is better. Either way, $2–$3 on every ride transforms your rideshare experience over time."

title: She said the second thing most riders don't know is that walking 2–3 blocks before requesting a ride can drop the price by $5–$15 — because surge pricing is zone-based, not city-wi
hook_spoken: She said the second thing most riders don't know is that walking 2–3 blocks before requesting a ride can drop the price by $5–$15 — because surge pricing is zone-based, not city-wi

She said the second thing most riders don't know is that walking 2–3 blocks before requesting a ride can drop the price by $5–$15 — because surge pricing is zone-based, not city-wide.

This is the trick she said saves her the most money on nights out.

"Surge pricing isn't applied to the entire city at once. It's applied by geographic zones — small hexagonal areas the algorithm uses to calculate local supply and demand. When you're standing outside a concert venue, a stadium, or a busy bar district at 11:30 PM, your zone has 500 people requesting rides and 12 available drivers. The surge multiplier spikes to 2x or 3x."

She said the zone next to you — literally 2–3 blocks away — often has a completely different multiplier.

"Walk 200–400 meters away from the venue or the bar strip. Open the app again. The fare often drops significantly because you've crossed into an adjacent zone with lower demand. You're still going to the same destination. The driver still picks you up. The ride still takes the same amount of time. But the starting fare is $8–$15 less because you requested from a zone the algorithm isn't surging."

She said this works because the surge calculation happens at the moment of request, based on your GPS location.

"The algorithm checks: where is the rider right now? What's the demand in this zone? What's the supply? It calculates the multiplier and shows you the fare. If you move 2 blocks and re-check, the algorithm recalculates based on the new zone. The demand at your new location is lower. The fare drops. It's the same ride. You just changed where you pressed the button."

She said she does this every single time she leaves a crowded area.

"After a concert, I never request from the venue. I walk 3 blocks toward a quieter street, then request. After a night out in a bar district, I walk to the edge of the neighborhood before opening the app. Three minutes of walking saves me $8–$15 every time. Over a year of going out twice a week, that's $800–$1,500 in savings from a 3-minute walk."

title: She said the seventh thing most riders don't use is the "Wait and Save" option — and it's the easiest discount on the platform.
hook_spoken: She said the seventh thing most riders don't use is the "Wait and Save" option — and it's the easiest discount on the platform.

She said the seventh thing most riders don't use is the "Wait and Save" option — and it's the easiest discount on the platform.

Both Uber and Lyft offer a ride option — often called "UberX Saver" or Lyft's equivalent — that gives you a lower fare in exchange for a longer pickup window. Instead of a driver arriving in 3–5 minutes, you agree to wait 10–20 minutes.

"UberX Saver is typically 15–30% cheaper than standard UberX. Same car. Same driver quality. Same route. Same destination. The only difference is you wait a few extra minutes for the driver to arrive. The app uses the extra time to find a driver who's already heading in your direction — which is more efficient for the driver and cheaper for you."

She said most riders never select this option because it's not the default.

"The app defaults to the standard UberX or Lyft option. Wait and Save is listed below it — sometimes you have to scroll down to see it. Most riders tap the first option and confirm without looking at alternatives. They don't realize that 2 inches of scrolling and 10 minutes of patience would save them $4–$8 per ride."

She said she uses Wait and Save for any ride where she's not in a rush.

"Going to the grocery store? Wait and Save. Heading to a friend's house on a Saturday afternoon? Wait and Save. Morning commute where I leave 15 minutes earlier than usual? Wait and Save. The only times I use standard pricing are when I'm late for something or when surge makes even the Saver option expensive. For every casual ride, the extra wait is worth the savings."

title: She said the sixth thing most riders don't know is that Uber and Lyft both offer subscription plans — and for frequent riders, they pay for themselves immediately.
hook_spoken: She said the sixth thing most riders don't know is that Uber and Lyft both offer subscription plans — and for frequent riders, they pay for themselves immediately.
transcript_30s:
She said the sixth thing most riders don't know is that Uber and Lyft both offer subscription plans — and for frequent riders, they pay for themselves immediately.

Uber One costs roughly $9.99/month. Lyft Pink costs roughly $9.99/month. Most riders have never heard of either.

"Uber One gives you 6–8% off every eligible UberX ride, reduced surge pricing when surge is active, $0 delivery fee on Uber Eats orders, and 5% off Uber Eats orders over $15. If you take 4–5 Uber rides per month, the discount on rides alone covers the subscription cost. Everything after that is pure savings. If you also use Uber Eats, it pays for itself in the first week."

She said Lyft Pink offers similar benefits.

"Lyft Pink gives you a percentage discount on every ride, priority airport pickups, relaxed cancellation fees, and exclusive promotions. For riders who take 10+ Lyft rides per month, Pink saves $15–$25/month after the subscription cost. That's $180–$300/year in net savings."

She said most riders don't subscribe because they don't know these plans exist.

"Neither Uber nor Lyft promotes these subscriptions aggressively in the main ride-booking flow. They're buried in the profile or settings menu. Most riders have opened the app hundreds of times and never seen them. But the math is simple: if you ride 3+ times per week on either platform, the subscription saves you more than it costs. Every month. Without changing anything about how you ride."

She said she subscribes to both.

"I have Uber One and Lyft Pink simultaneously. Total cost: $20/month. I comparison shop every ride between both apps. Whichever is cheaper gets my trip — and I'm getting a subscriber discount on top of the lower fare. Over a month, the combined subscriptions save me $40–$60 net. That's $480–$720/year in savings for $240/year in subscriptions. The math works for anyone who rides 4+ times per week."

title: She said the third thing most riders don't use is the "Schedule a Ride" feature — and it locks in a fare before surge pricing hits.
hook_spoken: She said the third thing most riders don't use is the "Schedule a Ride" feature — and it locks in a fare before surge pricing hits.
transcript_30s:
She said the third thing most riders don't use is the "Schedule a Ride" feature — and it locks in a fare before surge pricing hits.

Both Uber and Lyft let you schedule rides in advance — typically anywhere from 15 minutes to 30 days before your pickup time. Most riders think this is just a convenience feature for airport trips. She said it's actually a pricing tool.

"When you schedule a ride, the app locks in a fare estimate at the time of scheduling — not at the time of pickup. If you schedule your Friday night ride home at 2:00 PM when there's no surge, you lock in the non-surge fare. When 11:30 PM hits and the surge multiplier is 2.5x, your fare is still based on what you locked in earlier. Everyone else requesting at 11:30 PM is paying surge prices. You're not."

She said this doesn't work perfectly every time — the locked fare is an estimate, not a guarantee, and the final fare can adjust slightly based on actual route and traffic. But the savings compared to requesting during peak surge are significant.

"I schedule my rides home from nights out every single time. I schedule airport pickups 24 hours in advance. I schedule weekday morning commutes the night before if I know rush hour will be busy. The scheduled fare is almost always lower than the real-time fare during peak periods. It's not always the absolute floor price — but it consistently beats surge."

She said Uber's "Reserve" feature takes this even further.

"Uber Reserve lets you book a ride up to 90 days in advance and guarantees a driver will be assigned to you. The fare is locked. The driver is committed. There's no surge adjustment at pickup time. It costs a small premium over the base fare — usually $5–$8 — but on a night when surge would add $20–$30, the Reserve premium saves you $12–$22. For airport rides and event nights, it's the single smartest booking option most riders have never tried."

Thanks for reaching us,
We understand the concern,the cars moving across your map before you book aren't actual vehicles waiting for your request—they are visual placeholders generated by an optimistic algorithm designed to show general supply in your area. When you finally hit Confirm, Uber broadcasts your ride request to nearby drivers one by one. If those drivers decline the trip because of low pay rates, an inconvenient destination, or an upcoming break, the algorithm expands its search radius until an available driver accepts—which is often someone 20 to 25 minutes away. To minimize these delays, you can request your ride 5 to 10 minutes early to absorb the dispatch buffer, opt for a higher-tier ride like Uber Comfort to boost driver acceptance rates, or use Uber Reserve for time-sensitive trips to secure a driver in advance.

Vibe coding is real. 1 month later, Aura hits 15k MRR and 21.7k users.

I soloed this project from scratch and made a cursor for design. Our entire design team is using it daily and we don’t use Figma anymore. Here are a few tips for vibe coding your own app.

Don’t just vibe code, vibe design as well. Too many spend too little effort in design. AI likes to generate basic UIs, so make sure to provide templates, urls, images, figma, etc. Starting with a meh UI will permeate the rest of your app. That’s because AI uses the initial design as a blueprint. So, spend some time vibe designing components, styles, cards, buttons and use resources like 21st dev, tailwind, reactbits, uiverse, aura, etc.

Don’t just use Claude 4 Sonnet. 90% of my prompts are with Claude 4, but it’s not perfect. Sometimes, it gets blocked and repeat the same mistakes over and over. So I switch to Gemini 2.5 Pro or o3 for second opinions. I tried Opus but that didn’t solve harder problems, and the cost isn’t worth it.

Don’t expect to one-shot things. Those are the worst results because you won’t understand what the heck is going on. Instead, do incremental changes, read the logs and comments. Learn basic code and security. As your app gets more complex, this is even more crucial. Before you say that vibe coding apps are impossible when they’re big, Aura has 118k lines of code.

The context is in your brain. AI isn’t that good at knowing where things are. EVEN if you attach your entire codebase (costly!) or create rules, AI gets confused a lot. It doesn’t remember. 99% of the time, I prompt with a file or two attached. The best results I get are by starting with a simple file and let AI be the detective.

You gotta be creative at rephrasing/reframing your prompts. Most people quit at the first prompt. But often, you can only solve hard problems after the 3rd attempt. Know your vocabulary, seek alternatives, simplify your goals, make small jumps.

And honestly, that feels very plausible.

Because when an AI-generated `final_final_v12.py` takes production down at 3 AM, the person getting the call is not the AI.

It is the developer.

That is the part I find most revealing.

Every time the industry announces the end of developers, reality creates a fresh mess only developers can clean up.

So no, software engineers are not disappearing.

They are becoming the cleanup layer for AI-generated overconfidence.

What do you think AI is creating faster right now: code, or more work for the people still fixing everything?
